text:
Apollo 13: The Flight That Came Home

Apollo 13 left Florida on April 11, 1970, as the third mission planned to land humans on the Moon. By then the public had grown a little bored with the idea. Apollo 11 had made the first landing less than a year earlier, and Apollo 12 had followed in November. The networks skipped the broadcasts from Apollo 13's early days. That changed quickly.

The crew was commander Jim Lovell, a veteran of four spaceflights, lunar module pilot Fred Haise, and command module pilot Jack Swigert. Swigert was a late replacement. Ken Mattingly had been exposed to German measles days before launch, and flight surgeons judged him likely to fall ill during the mission. Swigert, the backup, took his seat with only a few days to prepare. The destination was the Fra Mauro highlands, and the plan was for Lovell and Haise to descend in the lunar module, Aquarius, while Swigert stayed in orbit aboard the command module, Odyssey.

For two days the flight was nearly routine. On the evening of April 13, about 56 hours in and some 200,000 miles from Earth, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the oxygen tanks in the service module. The tanks held supercooled liquid oxygen, which tends to settle and stratify, so the crew periodically ran fans inside them. Swigert threw the switch. A little over a minute later, the spacecraft shuddered with a loud bang.

Swigert reported, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it: "Houston, we've had a problem." On the ground, flight controllers first suspected their instruments. Readings were scattered and contradictory. Then the facts accumulated. One oxygen tank showed zero pressure. The second was draining. Two of the three fuel cells, which made the ship's electricity and drinking water from oxygen and hydrogen, were failing. Haise, looking out the window, saw a gas venting into space. Lovell recognized what that meant for the Moon. It was gone, and the question now was survival.

The cause, determined later, lay in the ship's history. The oxygen tank had been damaged on the ground before the flight. During a pre-launch test, a heater's thermostat switches were fused by a power supply they were not designed to handle. Ground crews never noticed. When Swigert switched on the fans, a spark in the damaged wiring ignited the Teflon insulation inside a tank of nearly pure oxygen. The tank ruptured and blew off a panel of the service module, crippling the second tank as well.

Flight director Gene Kranz and his teams had to decide fast. The obvious option, a direct abort, was impractical. It required using the service module's main engine, and nobody could trust a damaged service module. Instead, the controllers chose to use the lunar module as a lifeboat. Aquarius had its own oxygen, water, power, and engine. It was built to support two men for about two days on the lunar surface. Now it had to keep three alive for four.

The ship was on a trajectory that, left alone, would loop around the Moon and return toward Earth, though it would miss the planet by a wide margin. The crew first used Aquarius's descent engine to correct this. Then, after swinging around the far side of the Moon, they fired it again, a burn timed to speed the return home by roughly ten hours. During the lunar flyby, Apollo 13 passed about 158 miles above the surface and, at its farthest point, reached roughly 248,000 miles from Earth, the greatest distance humans have ever traveled from the planet. They had no time to enjoy it, though Lovell later remembered the Moon's far side passing silently below.

Powering down Odyssey was a careful operation in itself. Its batteries were needed for the final descent through the atmosphere and had to last. Swigert and the crew shut off nearly everything and moved into the lunar module. Electrical use in Aquarius was cut to a fraction of normal. To conserve water for cooling the electronics, the crew drank very little. Haise developed a fever and a urinary infection. Temperatures inside the spacecraft dropped to around 40 degrees Fahrenheit, and condensation formed on the walls. The men slept poorly, if at all, and rarely enough.

Then came a threat the designers had not anticipated. Carbon dioxide exhaled by three men began to build up in the small lunar module. Its lithium hydroxide canisters, which absorb the gas, would run out long before the trip ended. The command module held a supply of more canisters, but they were square, and the lunar module's scrubber took round ones. On the ground, engineers gathered the same kinds of items the crew had aboard, including plastic bags, cardboard, a spacesuit hose, and duct tape, and built an adapter. Capcom read the instructions up to the crew, step by step, and they assembled it. The carbon dioxide levels fell. This improvised device became one of the best-known pieces of engineering in the history of spaceflight.

Meanwhile, Ken Mattingly, the grounded astronaut, spent long hours in a simulator in Houston. The ship would need to be powered back up before reentry, and the normal procedure assumed a plentiful supply of electricity. Mattingly and the engineers wrote a new one that used far less, and it had to work the first time.

Navigation was another problem. With the guidance system shut down to save power, the crew had to make a mid-course correction by hand. They aimed by holding the Earth in a window, keeping its terminator in a fixed position. Lovell flew a burn manually, and the ship stayed on track. A trajectory that is a fraction of a degree too shallow bounces the spacecraft off the atmosphere, and one that is too steep burns it up.

On April 17, they started the final sequence. The service module was jettisoned first. As it drifted away, the crew photographed it and saw for the first time how badly it was hurt. A whole panel was missing, and equipment hung out of the gap. Lovell said so on the radio. Next they said goodbye to Aquarius, which had saved their lives. They released it shortly before reentry, and it burned up over the Pacific.

Odyssey, cold and dark and wet inside, was brought back to life, and Mattingly's procedure worked. The command module entered the atmosphere. The expected communications blackout, normally about three minutes, began. Controllers watched the clock. Nobody knew how the heat shield would hold after days of cold and the nearby explosion. The three minutes passed with no word. Then, after a long stretch, a voice came through. Swigert said, "OK, Joe," and the room, and a large part of the world, exhaled. Parachutes opened, and television showed the capsule swinging under three white canopies.

Apollo 13 splashed down in the South Pacific near Samoa on April 17, 1970, a little under six days after launch, and was recovered by the USS Iwo Jima. All three men were alive. They were tired, dehydrated, and thin. Haise was seriously ill, and Lovell had lost the better part of fifteen pounds. They had not landed on the Moon, and no one at the time called the mission a success in the way NASA had meant when it was planned. Yet it is often remembered as the agency's finest hour, when the ground and the crew improvised their way through a failure no one had trained for.

The investigation that followed redesigned the oxygen tanks and their wiring. Later Apollo missions flew with changes the accident had forced. Lovell never walked on the Moon, but he is remembered for the voyage he made without doing so. The Apollo 13 story has lasted because people solved problem after problem, in real time, to bring three men home.
